summary: A seven-day consecration process is prescribed for Aaron and his sons, involving washing, clothing, oil, sacrificed animals, applied blood, and a restricted meal. Daily morning and evening offerings then establish an ongoing pattern, concluding with God's promise to meet Israel and dwell among the people brought out of Egypt.
whyItMatters: The chapter describes repeated physical acts that prepare both the priesthood and altar for service. Its closing promise explains why the elaborate ritual matters within Exodus: rescue leads toward God's dwelling among Israel.

context.author: Exodus does not name its final author. It records Moses writing particular covenant material; traditional Mosaic attribution and modern accounts of composition are distinguished in the book briefing.
context.audience: Israel remembering its rescue from Egypt and its obligations as a covenant community. The chapter does not identify an individual dedicatee.
context.date: The narrative places these events at Sinai after the departure from Egypt. The date of the events and the history of the book’s composition are separate, debated questions.
context.setting: Sinai instructions for the future ordination at the Tent of Meeting and the altar's continuing service.
context.literaryForm: A ritual sequence for priestly consecration followed by daily offering requirements and a statement of divine purpose.

before.text: The garments have been specified, including Aaron's memorial stones and the clothing required for safe approach. This chapter describes how the wearers and altar are to be set apart.

here.text: Track the bull, the two rams, the portions burned or eaten, and the seven-day repetition before the instructions broaden into daily service.

after.text: The next instructions add the incense altar, census payment, washing basin, and specially restricted oil and incense.

outline.heading: Preparation, washing, garments, and oil
outline.note: Aaron and his sons are dressed and anointed for their continuing office.

outline.heading: The bull as a sin offering
outline.note: Blood goes to the altar and selected parts burn there, while the rest is burned outside the camp.

outline.heading: The first ram as a whole burnt offering
outline.note: Its blood and body are assigned their specified treatment.

outline.heading: The second ram and priestly portions
outline.note: Blood marks bodies and garments, and selected food is waved, burned, or assigned as a portion.

outline.heading: Garments, meal, and seven days of consecration
outline.note: The process regulates succession, sacred food, and repeated cleansing of the altar.

outline.heading: Daily offerings and promised presence
outline.note: Morning and evening sacrifice leads into God’s promise to meet and dwell with Israel.

keyVerses.text: Then you shall kill the ram, and take some of its blood, and put it on the tip of the right ear of Aaron, and on the tip of the right ear of his sons, and on the thumb of their right hand, and on the big toe of their right foot; and sprinkle the blood around on the altar.
keyVerses.why: The consecration visibly marks the priests’ bodies with the blood of a killed animal.

keyVerses.text: Seven days you shall make atonement for the altar, and sanctify it; and the altar shall be most holy. Whatever touches the altar shall be holy.
keyVerses.why: The altar’s preparation requires a full seven-day process of atonement and consecration.

keyVerses.text: They shall know that I am Yahweh their God, who brought them out of the land of Egypt, that I might dwell among them: I am Yahweh their God.
keyVerses.why: The final statement explicitly connects departure from Egypt with God dwelling among the people.

questions.question: What happens before the animals are sacrificed?
questions.answer: Aaron and his sons are brought to the tent entrance and washed; Aaron is dressed in his garments and anointed, and his sons are clothed. The sequence prepares their bodies and office before describing the sacrificial actions.

questions.question: How are the bull and first ram treated differently?
questions.answer: The bull is called a sin offering: selected fat is burned at the altar, while flesh, skin, and dung burn outside the camp. The first ram is a burnt offering whose whole prepared body is burned on the altar, so the animals are not interchangeable within the rite.

questions.question: Does the text explain the meaning of blood on the ear, thumb, and toe?
questions.answer: It commands application to those right-side body parts and then blood and oil on the priests and their garments. The acts are part of making them holy, but separate explanations such as consecrating hearing, work, and walking are interpretive associations rather than explanations supplied in these verses.

questions.question: What is a “wave offering” here?
questions.answer: Selected animal portions and bread are placed in the priests' hands and waved before God before being burned, and a breast portion is also waved. The term names a presented offering within the ritual; the text does not detail every motion or its direction.

questions.question: Who may eat the consecration meal?
questions.answer: Aaron and his sons eat the ram and bread at the tent entrance, while a stranger is excluded because the food is holy. Leftovers must be burned by morning, preserving the food’s restricted purpose and use.

questions.question: Does making atonement for the altar imply that an object has committed a moral offense?
questions.answer: The instructions speak of cleansing and consecrating the altar through atonement and anointing over seven days. In this setting the language concerns preparing an object for holy use, so it extends beyond a person’s moral wrongdoing.

questions.question: How do the daily offerings relate to the chapter’s conclusion?
questions.answer: A lamb is offered morning and evening with flour, oil, and wine, creating continuing service at the meeting place. God then promises to sanctify the place and priesthood and dwell among Israel, giving the recurring acts a stated purpose within the rescue story.

glossary.def: Apply the specified oil as part of setting a priest or sacred object apart.
A portion presented by a waving action before God within the prescribed ritual.
The ritual action connected here with consecrating the priests and cleansing the altar for holy use.
